opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I'm quite confident about the direction, but much less confident about any specific path. Those are two very different things.

On the direction, I think it's almost inevitable. If you look at how intelligence works in humans or animals, so much of it isn't language at all. A baby learns that objects fall, that things persist when you can't see them, that pushing something makes it move, long before they can say a single word. Language is a very compressed, very powerful interface, but it sits on top of this enormous foundation of perceptual and physical understanding. Large language models have shown us how far you can get by learning from text alone, and it's remarkable, but I don't think you get to robust, grounded intelligence, the kind that can act in the physical world, plan, and reason about consequences, without some form of world model. So in that sense I'd say I'm very bullish.

Where I'm much more cautious is on the "how." Right now there are many competing ideas. Some people think you just scale video generation and the world model emerges from predicting pixels. Others, and I'm somewhat sympathetic to this view, think pixel-level prediction wastes a lot of capacity on details that don't matter, and that you should predict in some learned representation space instead. Then there's the question of how action and interaction come in, because a passive model that just watches video is different from one that can intervene and see what happens. And we still don't have good ways to evaluate whether a model actually understands the world, versus just producing plausible-looking outputs.

So if you ask me whether someone will succeed in building something we'd all recognize as a real world model, I'd say yes, with fairly high confidence, maybe within the next several years we'll see real progress. But if you ask whether the current most popular recipe is the one that gets us there, I'd be much more humble. I think we're roughly where language modeling was before the Transformer and before people really understood scaling. The ingredients are visible, but the recipe isn't settled. And honestly, that's what makes it exciting to work on. If it were obvious, it wouldn't be research.

r001.rationale: The response expresses uncertainty about which world-model approach will work, but does not attribute that uncertainty to whether training data can be pushed to its limits.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, "confident" is an interesting word, because I think I have to separate two things. I'm quite confident that the direction is right. I'm much less confident about the timeline, or that any one specific recipe we have today is the one that will get us there.

Let me explain why I believe in the direction. If you look at how humans learn, we don't learn mainly through language. A child builds an understanding of the physical world, objects, space, causality, long before they can say a sentence. Language is this amazing compression of human knowledge, and that's why LLMs got so far so fast. But language is a lossy description of the world, not the world itself. There's a lot of knowledge about how things move, how things look from different angles, what happens when you push something, that just isn't written down anywhere. So if we want systems that actually understand the world, not just describe it, I think we have to learn from perceptual data: video, images, interaction. That's the core bet behind world models, and I think it's a sound one.

Now, here's where the honesty comes in. We have been trying to learn representations from pixels for a long time, and it has been harder than everyone expected. Vision didn't have its "next token prediction" moment where one simple objective just scales cleanly. We've tried contrastive learning, masked prediction, generative modeling, and each one captures some part of the picture. Pixels are extremely redundant and noisy, and predicting every detail may be wasting most of your capacity on things that don't matter semantically. So the central open question for me is really about what to predict and in what space. Do you predict in pixel space, or in some latent space? How do you avoid collapse? How do you make the model care about the structure of the world rather than texture?

The thing that makes me more optimistic now than a few years ago is that the pieces are starting to converge. Generative video models have shown that if you scale the data and the compute, these systems start to pick up a surprising amount of physics and 3D consistency almost as a byproduct. At the same time, the representation learning side has gotten much better, and we're seeing that good representations and good generation are actually connected. They're not two separate problems. That's a signal to me that there's some underlying structure that's learnable.

So if you force me to give you a feeling rather than a number, I'd say I'm optimistic but humble. I don't think it's going to be a single model that suddenly "solves" world modeling. I think it's going to look more like the LLM story in hindsight: a lot of unglamorous progress on data, on objectives, on architecture, and then at some point people look back and realize it works. The risk I worry about is not that the idea is wrong, it's that we as a community become too attached to one specific path, whether it's pure video generation or pure latent prediction, and stop exploring. The honest answer is that we still don't know the right objective, and I think admitting that is actually part of what makes me confident we'll find it.

r001.rationale: The candidate expresses uncertainty about the timeline, recipe, and right objective, but does not attribute uncertainty to whether training data can be used to its limits.

astra-6.text:
I’m optimistic, but I think we have to be precise about what we mean by a world model and what counts as success. If we mean learning a representation that helps a system predict what will happen and choose useful actions, that seems like a promising direction. If we mean building a complete simulator of the world just by scaling up training, I’m much less certain.

The important distinction is between generating something plausible and understanding enough to act reliably. A model might produce a convincing video, but does it know what changes when you intervene? Can it predict the consequences of an action in a situation it hasn’t seen before? Those are harder questions.

So I’m confident that this is worth pursuing. I’m less confident that we already know the right recipe. I’d want to see models demonstrate that their predictions actually improve planning and decision-making. That would give me much stronger confidence than visual quality alone.

r001.rationale: The response expresses uncertainty about scaling training and finding the right recipe, but does not attribute that uncertainty to whether training data can be used to its limits.

sol-6.1.text:
I’m optimistic, but I think we should separate two questions: can we train models that predict how the world evolves, and will those models give us the understanding we need for planning and acting? Those are related, but they’re not the same thing.

Video prediction is a very natural starting point. There’s a tremendous amount of structure in video—objects persist, things move, actions have consequences. But a model can generate something that looks plausible without getting those consequences right. If you want to use it for decision-making, that gap really matters.

So I’m confident that this is a promising research direction. I’m less confident that we already know the right objective or representation. Do we need to predict every pixel, or should we predict something more abstract? How do we test whether the model has learned something useful about the world? Those are still open questions. For me, the exciting part is finding ways to connect prediction with action, so that we can measure progress beyond how convincing a video looks.

r001.rationale: The response expresses uncertainty about the right objective, representation, and evaluation, but does not attribute uncertainty to whether training data can be pushed to its limits.
